gloss: seal · stamp · print — and, in Buddhist texts, the mudrā
formNote: The Shuowen: 印，執政所持信也。从爪从卩 — “what those in office hold as proof: from hand, from 卩.” Early forms show a hand over a kneeling person, which many read as the same word as 抑, “to press down”.
summary: A seal pressed into clay or onto paper, and so a print or a mark. Buddhist translators gave it mudrā, the sealing gesture of the hands; Xuanzang wrote 印度 for India and glossed it as “moon”.
placement: On the right of the band, beside 實: the seal that marks a thing as real. (Placement is a design choice, not a claim.)

oc.note: † Baracus, from general knowledge; not yet checked against B–S 2014.

satellites.title: Seal of the Hands
satellites.evidence: Mudrā means “seal, stamp” in Sanskrit, and also a ritual gesture; 印 renders it, so 手印 and 印相 name the gestures of the hands in Buddhist images and practice. One word covers the stamp and the gesture in both languages.

satellites.title: India, Named for the Moon
satellites.evidence: Xuanzang, Datang Xiyu ji ch. 2: 舊云身毒，或曰賢豆，今從正音，宜云印度。印度者，唐言月 — “formerly called Shendu or Xiandou; by the correct sound it should be Yindu, and Yindu in Tang speech means ‘moon’.” He hears Sanskrit indu, “moon”, in the name.
satellites.caveat: The name derives from Sindhu, the Indus; the moon is Xuanzang’s gloss, not the etymology.

satellites.title: A Hand Pressing Down
satellites.evidence: Oracle-bone forms of 印 show a hand (爪) over a kneeling figure (卩), pressing down; many palaeographers take 印 and 抑, “to press, to restrain”, as one word in origin. A seal is a pressing.
satellites.caveat: The 印 / 抑 identification is a common modern reading, drafted by Baracus from general knowledge.
gaps: Name a palaeographic source for 印 = 抑.
